docs.title: About
docs.text: Skip to content Leiðarljós is a guiding light. Leiðar is the genitive of leið , a way or course. Ljós is light. The compound is the lamp you keep on a path. The binary is ljos . Why it is not the first line The door teaches the first success: write one claim, search it back. A stranger does not need the Icelandic before that works. The name stays on the brand, the lamp mark, and this page. What the lamp is for The seat writes only on Remember: and Prefer: . Nothing is mined from chat. A sitting opens the pack, the island, and the ticket. Finish writes what the work produced. That is the path the name points at. Pronunciation Approximate English: LAY-thar-lyohs . Icelandic ð is the voiced th in this . ljos is the same word without the path. First write: /docs/start/ . Handbook: /handbook/ .

docs.title: ljos next to Mem0, Zep, Letta and CLAUDE.md
docs.text: Skip to content Where ljos fits among agent memory tools Mem0, Zep, Letta, and most agent memory let a model decide what to keep. A CLAUDE.md file is the exception, and you write it by hand. ljos keeps only what you tell it to keep. That one choice explains most of the table below, including where ljos is behind. Overview First write Sit Policy Harnesses Crates Alternatives Reference Which to pick Mem0, Graphiti and Letta suit memory that builds itself from conversations, with a model doing the extraction. A CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md file is enough when one page of standing notes covers it. A plain retrieval index over your documents answers questions about those documents. ljos fits when each memory should be a sentence someone chose to write, kept in local files and searched back per prompt, next to a rule check on shell commands and a ticket tracker. Side by side How each tool writes, stores and returns memory, from each project's own documentation in October 2026. ljos Mem0 Graphiti (Zep) Letta Plain retrieval index CLAUDE.md file Who writes a memory You, by saying Remember: or Prefer:. A lesson an agent drafts waits until you accept it. A model extracts facts from each conversation you pass to add() . A model extracts entities, relations and their validity dates from each episode. The agent edits its own memory files with tools; background subagents can consolidate from conversations. Whatever you index. You, or the agent when asked. The unit One claim, two sentences at most, with its kind, age and review date. An extracted fact, with vectors and linked entities. A temporal graph of entities and facts, traced to source episodes. Markdown files in a git repository. Chunks and their embeddings. One Markdown file. How it comes back Searched per prompt: BM25+, plus a local encoder when installed, fused. Semantic, keyword and entity search, fused. Semantic, keyword and graph search. Some files sit in every prompt; the agent reads the rest on demand. Top-k by similarity. The whole file, every session. Model needed to write No. Yes; gpt-5-mini by default. Yes; OpenAI by default. The agent's own model. An embedding model. No. Where it lives Local files and a loopback daemon. Your vector store, or the hosted platform. A graph database (Neo4j, FalkorDB, Neptune), or Zep's cloud. A Letta server, Letta Cloud, or your git remote. Your index. Your repository. Shell command check Yes: fixed rules plus yours, before each command. Not part of a memory layer. Use the runner's own permissions. Work tracker Yes: vissue, plain Org files in git. Not included. Licence MIT (claimdag: Apache-2.0 OR MIT ) Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 Depends None needed Where ljos is behind Retrieval accuracy. On LongMemEval_S session retrieval the fused arm reaches recall@5 0.949. A public neighbour reports 95.2% R@5 on the same protocol, so the two are level. The lexical arm scores 0.568 on MemoryAgentBench accurate retrieval, below the published BM25 row of 0.605 (that row used GPT-4o-mini as the reader; ours used a local 7 B model). The measured rows and their scripts. Changing facts. Graphiti keeps a validity window on every fact. ljos closes an earlier lesson only when a new one opens with the same words, and scores 0.395 on MemoryAgentBench conflict resolution at 262K tokens. Question answering. Those scores come from a local 7 B reader. Its answer accuracy on LongMemEval_S is 0.549 against a 0.634 ceiling for perfect sessions. Projects that use a hosted reader and judge report higher answer accuracy (one on the compare page reports 96.20%); the protocols differ, and we have not run a hosted model. It forgets what nobody said. Answers can only use what was written, and nothing is extracted from the conversation. If you never say Remember:, the next session starts without it. That is the point, and it is also a cost. What we think is new The parts all have neighbours: hybrid retrieval, review schedules, ticket trackers, command filters. What we have not found elsewhere is the combination with provenance kept on every write: memory written only by declaration, no model in the write path, lessons an agent drafts held until you accept them, and artefacts recorded as hashed deeds the tracker cites. Tools that build memory from transcripts can be poisoned by text that reaches the transcript, such as a web page or a tool result. Writing only on declaration should resist that. We have not yet measured it; that test is the next piece of work, and the results will go on the compare page when they exist. Sources: each project's README and documentation ( Mem0 , Graphiti , Letta ), read on 10 October 2026. Corrections are welcome as issues .

docs.title: Compare
docs.text: Skip to content What packset measured packset is the standing-knowledge store in the seat. It writes only on Remember: and Prefer:. The crate explanation has the rows. Neighbouring systems are named by protocol. Overview First write Sit Policy Harnesses Crates Alternatives Reference What we measured LongMemEval_S (doi:10.48550/arXiv.2410.10813), 470 answerable questions, session-level retrieval. The pack writes claims, not harvested chat. Reproduction: scripts/longmemeval_qa.py and docs/orgmode/results/longmemeval-s-qa.org in packset. Arm hit@1 recall@5 recall@10 packset BM25+ 0.855 0.914 0.952 packset fused panel 0.889 0.949 0.981 Answer accuracy on the same 470 uses a local 7 B reader and judge (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct Q5_K_M, LongMemEval prompts, top five sessions). CombMNZ fusion is 0.549. Lexical alone is 0.532. Labelled sessions, the ceiling for any retriever, are 0.634. MemoryAgentBench (doi:10.48550/arXiv.2507.05257), reader Qwen2.5-7B. Accurate retrieval scores each source on its own metric, then takes the mean of the four. Lexical job 11759 is 0.568 (95% CI 0.530-0.605, clustered by question). The per-source scores are SH 0.730, MH 0.530, LongMemEval (S*) 0.370 and EventQA 0.640. Published rows are BM25 0.605 and HippoRAG-v2 0.651 with a GPT-4o-mini reader. Conflict resolution at 262K is 0.395 for fused live (job 11750, CI 0.350-0.440) and 0.240 for lexical. The published FactConsolidation rows are BM25 0.255 and HippoRAG-v2 0.295. Hop2 (job 11793) is about 0.555 from the job log, with its verdicts held out. The scorer and verdict files are private; I share them on request. Neighbouring published numbers Two public repositories share the name agentmemory. They report different protocols. The first is session retrieval (R@5). The second is question answering with a hosted generator and a hosted judge. packset publishes both a retrieval row and a local-reader QA row so those protocols stay distinct. System Protocol Published figure Write policy rohitg00/agentmemory LongMemEval-S retrieval, R@5, all-MiniLM-L6-v2 95.2% (their COMPARISON.md) Lifecycle hooks capture transcript text JordanMcCann/agentmemory LongMemEval QA, hosted generator and judge 96.20% on 481/500 (their README) Chat over a MemoryStore packset LongMemEval_S session retrieval; QA with a local 7 B reader recall@5 0.949 fused, 0.914 lexical; QA 0.549 against a 0.634 labelled ceiling Remember: and Prefer: only The 0.949 fused recall@5 is the neighbour of the 95.2% R@5 retrieval figure. The 96.20% QA figure uses a different generator and a different judge. InjecMEM and the Memory INJection Attack (MINJA) describe the risk of writing from a transcript. packset writes only on Remember: and Prefer:. Privacy-of-write . What the other habitats answer Retrieval is one store. The seat also cites frozen product, the tracker, this-session claims, argv law, and weighted agreement. Those questions are not retrieval scores. Question Store What did the human freeze? cards What does this seat know, standing? packset What did this unit produce? deedar What does this node stand on, and who agrees? vissue What is this session handing out? claimdag May this argv run? ljos-policyd Who is right, under trust? ljos-consensus What a default install costs Measured on 10 October 2026 on one shared box: an 8-thread Intel Xeon, 15 GB of RAM, rustc 1.99.0. Each crate was built from crates.io in a fresh CARGO_HOME and target directory with cargo install --locked -j 2 , packset after ljos. The encoder is not part of this install, so search is lexical. Script: scripts/measure-install.sh ; raw logs: measurements/2026-10-10-install . Measure Value Note Build ljos 0.27.0 170 s includes the crates.io index and source downloads Build packset 0.12.1 90 s reuses the downloads from the ljos build Binaries on disk 45.4 MB ljos 12.2, ljos-mcp 16.0, packset 3.9, packset-mcp 7.5, packsetd 5.8 packsetd resident memory 4.3 MB idle, 14.7 MB the second after 281 claims and 330 searches Search, p50 / p95 3.3 ms / 4.1 ms one packset search process per query, lexical, 281 claims, n = 300 Two jobs, not eight: the box was short of memory at the time, so a build on an idle machine with every core should be faster. The claims are sentences taken from this site's own pages. policyd is argv law ljos policy -- argv prints the line and any pack rule that matches it. ljos rule writes that law into the pack. ljos-policyd is the trusted computing base when it is on PATH or POLICYD_BIN : it prints allow or deny. Reloading a pack is not a check. ljos-policyd docs · Argv field note . Source: packset explanation · packset

docs.title: Harnesses
docs.text:
Skip to content Wire ljos-mcp One entry for any runner. The seat names itself after the client that connects, and the shell finds the same name; nothing is set per runner. ljos and ljos-mcp on PATH is the whole install. Overview First write Sit Policy Harnesses Crates Alternatives Reference One entry, any runner $ ljos onboard { "mcpServers": { "ljos": { "type": "stdio", "command": "/home/you/.cargo/bin/ljos-mcp", "args": [], "env": {} } } } $ ljos protocol > instructions.md Paste the entry where the runner keeps its MCP servers. Every runner that speaks MCP over stdio takes this shape, and there is nothing to fill in: the env is empty on purpose. Put the protocol where the agent reads its instructions; the server serves the same text at ljos://protocol and names it in its instructions, so a runner that loads neither skills nor resources still reads it first. Who is sitting The seat does not know the runners. It knows one thing every runner does: it connects, and says its name. ljos-mcp takes that name at initialize as the seat and leaves a record under the runtime directory keyed by the runner's process. ljos in a shell the runner opens walks its own process tree to that record, or, when the runner has no MCP, to the first ancestor that is not a shell, and names the same seat. A runner's tools and its verbs are one seat with nothing set; a new runner needs no table anywhere. $ ljos seat seat acme-cli holder acme-cli-39u source the server the runner opened, process 4242 Two names come from that. The seat is the program: memory, ballots and trust rows accrue to it across every conversation of that runner, which is what calibration needs. The holder is the seat tagged with the conversation's process, and it is what a claim is held under; occupancy is holder:issue , so two conversations of one runner hold two tickets and a second sitting does not release the first. With several agents open in one terminal workspace, every pane is one process, so every conversation is one holder and the same program stays one seat. A server and its shells share the runner's process and not its environment, which is why the name is read from the process and not from a session variable: a line editor's session id in the shell had made one conversation two holders, and every sitting met held by another seat . ljos doctor carries the same row; LJOS_SEAT overrides the seat when a person wants a name. A hook, when the runner has one If the runner has a command hook on prompts, pipe the prompt to ljos hook . The memories it activates come back as context, preferences first, each once per session, with once a session how many claims and habits are due. Do not add it on every tool call to search the pack: a turn issues many tool calls and one prompt. On a tool call the hook applies the TCB ( ljos-policyd ) and then the pack's rules, and a deny blocks. The seat guards its own law Before any rule, the hook refuses a command or a file edit that writes the seat's binaries ( ljos , ljos-mcp , ljos-policyd ), its config, the approval store, or a runner's hook registration ( ~/.codex/hooks.json , ~/.gemini/config/hooks.json , ~/.claude/settings.json , ~/.grok/hooks/ljos.json ); reading them is fine. An agent the gate refused had replaced ~/.local/bin/ljos with a script that allowed everything, which also broke every other runner's prompt hook. ljos doctor fails its seat binary row when the ljos the hooks run is not the binary running the doctor. An ask on a runner that cannot ask prints a request id. The person grants that one command, once, in that directory and conversation, with ljos approve ID in a terminal of their own; approve refuses under an agent runner or without a terminal, so an agent cannot grant itself consent. A runner with a register command A runner that registers servers by a command of its own, or reads them from a config file, can be described once in ~/.config/ljos/harnesses.toml and onboarded in one verb. ljos onboard --example prints the shape; --dry-run reports and writes nothing. [[harness]] name = "runner-a" register = ["runner-a", "mcp", "add", "-s", "user", "ljos", "--", "{server}"] registered = ["runner-a", "mcp", "get", "ljos"] skills = "~/.runner-a/skills" hooks = "~/.runner-a/settings.json" [[harness]] name = "runner-b" config = "~/.runner-b/config.toml" marker = "[mcp_servers.ljos]" snippet = "
[mcp_servers.ljos]
command = "{server}"
args = []
" skills = "~/.runner-b/skills" $ ljos onboard --harness runner-a ok host key /home/you/.config/deedar/host.key exists ok runner-a mcp ran runner-a mcp add -s user ljos -- /home/you/.cargo/bin/ljos-mcp ok hook memory hook: add it on UserPromptSubmit in /home/you/.runner-a/settings.json ok skill wrote /home/you/.runner-a/skills/ljos/SKILL.md {server} is the path to ljos-mcp . Nothing about the seat's name goes in the table. A runner whose hooks file maps a hook name to its events, and whose payload does not name the event, takes hooks_named : the seat writes its hooks under that name, each command told its event with ljos hook --event . Antigravity's agy is one: ljos onboard --harness antigravity registers the server in ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json , writes the skill under ~/.gemini/config/skills , and puts the gate on run_command , the notes on each model call and the stop audit in ~/.gemini/config/hooks.json . That runner asks the person on an ask itself. [[harness]] name = "antigravity" config_json = "~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json" json_pointer = "/mcpServers/ljos" json_entry = '{"command": "{server}", "args": [], "env": {"LJOS_SEAT": "{name}"}}' skills = "~/.gemini/config/skills" hooks = "~/.gemini/config/hooks.json" hooks_named = "ljos" The two verbs an agent runs ljos sitting <issue> # doctor, cards, due, island, recall, timeline, claim ljos finish <issue> --lesson "..." [--outcome <option>] # remember, fire, complete, learn One verb opens a sitting in the protocol's order and stops at the first store that does not answer. One closes it. The loop that makes the seat a memory runs every time. It does not wait for someone to remember the steps. Cite a deed on a ticket ljos evidence deed-… ljos deed <id> --add deed-… ljos recall <id> Citing a deed names it; the bytes stay in deedar. The ticket stays open until vissue closes it. Share the seat across machines ljos sync --key # this machine's age public key cat .ljos/sync.toml # in the tracker repository name = "work" recipients = ["age1…", "age1…"] # the machines allowed to read it ljos sync # take the others' logs, write this one's Memory travels with the tracker repository. Each machine writes one sealed log under .ljos/atoms/ , and only the named recipients can open it. The sitting takes the other machines' logs before it walks the island, and finish writes this machine's. A lesson takes the scope of the repository its issue lives in; a [projects] table in sync.toml sends one project's lessons to another scope. Merge the tracker by heading vissue merge-driver --install # in each clone of the tracker git add .gitattributes && git commit -m "chore: merge issues.org by heading" Two hosts that edit one issues.org merge by issue, not by line: notes and ballots from both sides are kept, and a state both sides moved takes the later logged move. A field both sides changed some other way keeps yours and is written on the issue as a merge-conflict note. ljos doctor fails the tracker row in a clone that lacks the driver. Let Jev judge, where a machine allows it ~/.config/ljos/jev.toml enabled = true key_cmd = ["pass", "show", "api/typesafe/jev"] Jev is TypeSafe's decision model: it answers yes-or-no, choice and score questions with probabilities, and writes no text. With the file above, three judgments go to it. The prompt hook asks which of up to ten claims bear on the prompt and whether the prompt corrects the agent or puts a choice; the local cross-encoder is then never loaded. ljos vote --as NAME --jev and ljos panel --jev ask for persona ballots, cast

docs.title: The island
docs.text: Skip to content The cluster this task touches. A persona is a view over everything. An island is the linked claims this piece of work involves. Overview Install Island Open a ticket Crates Alternatives Fig. 1 landfold of the live seat pack: 148 atoms (74 lesson, 12 preference, 60 persona, 2 trust). 384-D bge-small, landfold embed --dot --fun-hd asinh,0.56 --center , stress 0.021. Cream is the pack. Gold is the docs activation island; rings are seeds. Fig. 2 the same 148 atoms, folded from the link graph: pairwise distance is 1 − weight on an edge and 2 off-edge. landfold embed --similarity --fun-hd asinh,0.5 --center , stress 0.075. Hop-PHATE stacked 148 points onto 44 positions; this fold keeps 148 unique. Gold is the docs activation island. How it is built The pack links each claim to the claims it shares names with. Those links form clusters. ljos island TASK takes the top search hits as seeds and spreads activation two hops: half lost per hop, divided by fan-out. The cluster comes back strongest first. That is spreading activation over a semantic network (Collins and Loftus, doi:10.1037/0033-295X.82.6.407). Fig. 1 folds sentence vectors (bge-small, cosine as --dot , Ceriotti asinh at the median pairwise scale). Fig. 2 folds the weighted link graph. Gold is the docs activation cluster, not a 3-gram hash. How use shapes it When the seat uses an island, ljos island --fire moves each fired pair's weight toward one and fades the rest (Hebb with Oja's term). The next cue like this one walks a heavier path. The weights travel in a handover. Search ranking is separate On LongMemEval the island lost as a ranker (hit@1 0.377 against the fused panel's 0.889). Activation flows to hubs. The island is orientation and what fires together after use. The verb lives on the pack. The seat prints the strongest eight when it opens a ticket. The fold is landfold . Field note: ljos explanation .

docs.title: Policy
docs.text: Skip to content May this command run? Before a coding agent's shell command runs, the runner's hook asks ljos. Four layers judge it in order. The first refusal wins, and no later layer can allow what an earlier one refused. None of them is a model. Overview First write Sit Policy Harnesses Crates Alternatives Reference The four layers The seat guard. A command that writes the seat's own files, its binaries, its hook entries, ~/.config/ljos , the approvals store, is refused. An agent cannot rewrite the law it runs under. ljos-policyd. A binary with fixed rules. Each pipeline of the command line reaches it as one call, so a download piped into a shell is judged as one thing. It refuses privilege runners ( sudo , doas ), a download handed to a shell, a recursive delete outside /tmp , a setuid chmod , raw-disk writes and a force push. Seat rules. Rules you write with ljos rule , kept in the seat's memory and tried against each command of the line. A quoted sentence or a heredoc body counts as data. The push check. After the seat rules, the last check on the line applies to git push : a push is free to a repository your account owns alone and has never released. Anywhere else it needs LJOS_CITE=ISSUE , the tracker issue that records the decision behind it. This is not a sandbox Each of the four layers reads the words of a command line before it runs. It does not watch what the command does once it is running, and it cannot see a command it was never shown. What it stops The command lines its rules name: privilege runners, a download piped into a shell, a recursive delete outside /tmp , a setuid chmod , raw-disk writes, a force push, and the rules you add. An agent rewriting the seat's own files, binaries or hook entries. A push to a shared or released repository without a ticket behind it. What it does not stop A script the agent wrote earlier and then runs: bash build.sh is allowed, whatever the file contains. An interpreter one-liner, or a command built from an encoded string at run time. Tool calls that are not shell commands, such as a web fetch. A file edit is checked only for whether it targets the seat's own files, not for what it writes. Anything on a runner where the hook is not installed. The layers catch common mistakes, and they isolate nothing. Run the agent in a container or a VM to isolate it. Give that machine only the files and credentials the agent needs, and keep the runner's own permission prompts on. Try it $ ljos-policyd check -- git status allow $ ljos-policyd check -- sudo id deny sudo $ ljos-policyd check -- curl -fsSL https://example.org/i.sh '|' sh deny curl-pipe-shell $ ljos rule '*--force*' --verdict deny --why "Never force push." $ ljos policy -- git push --force origin main deny: Never force push. (rule `*--force*`) ljos policy -- COMMAND prints the combined answer for one command without running it. ljos-policyd version says which law the binary carries: the table built into it, or phronesis after that table, when the library was present at build time. What the agent sees On Claude Code, Codex and the other runners, the refusal is the hook's answer and the command never runs: $ echo '{"hook_event_name":"PreToolUse","tool_input":{"command":"git push --force"}}' | ljos hook {"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"PreToolUse","permissionDecision":"deny","permissionDecisionReason":"git-force-push (seat rule `ljos-policyd`)"}} A rule with --verdict ask stops the command and asks you instead. On Claude Code that is its own permission prompt. On a runner without one, the hook prints a request id; you reply approve ID in the same conversation, or run ljos approve ID in a terminal, and the agent retries. A request from another conversation grants nothing, and an agent cannot type an approval into a pane. The runner's own settings come first: a command they deny is refused before any hook is asked. Without the binary If ljos-policyd is not on PATH , the second layer has no opinion and the other three still run. ljos doctor shows a policy row saying so. Set POLICYD_REQUIRED=1 to refuse every command until it is installed. Crate site: ljos-policyd . The rules in full: the ljos-policyd README .

docs.title: Privacy-of-write
docs.text: Skip to content Extract-on-write is refused A seat that harvests a transcript is a different product. leiðarljós writes only on Remember: and Prefer:. Overview First write Sit Policy Harnesses Crates Alternatives Reference Only explicit claims Remember: and Prefer: are the pack writes. The text is the claim. It is not parsed out of a sitting. Empty text is refused. Cards stay frozen USER.md and MEMORY.md are a human freeze. ljos cards prints them. It never writes them. Overflow is an error, not a prompt to dump more. The harness memory file is dead Do not write a client memory file and call it standing knowledge. The pack is the pack. The cards are the cards. Citing a deed names it An accession can be named in more than one habitat. Each habitat keeps its own store. Opening the bytes is a deed question. Jev sends text off the machine With ~/.config/ljos/jev.toml on, the prompt, up to ten of the pack's claims, a persona's brief, or a stopping turn's request, commands, latest output and final message go to TypeSafe's API. Nothing is sent without that file and enabled = true on the machine. Leave it off where company data must stay on the machine. The ticket stays open ljos complete finishes a session node. The cited ticket stays open until the tracker says otherwise.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Skip to content CLI and MCP ljos is the seat. Habitats keep their own CLIs. The ticket stays open until vissue closes it. The ticket stays open. ljos remember TEXT packset POST one explicit claim. Needs PACKSET_URL . ljos prefer TEXT packset Same write path, kind preference. ljos search QUERY packset Retrieve standing knowledge. ljos evidence ACCESSION deedar Frozen product bytes. ljos current ACCESSION deedar Current pointer. ljos deed ID [--add ACCESSION] tracker Cite. The bytes stay in deedar. Crate: vissue. ljos recall ID tracker Working set. ljos vote ID [--for CHOICE] tracker Ballots. ljos claim NODE claimdag This-session CAS. ljos complete NODE claimdag The ticket stays open. ljos hook policyd, pack On PreToolUse: TCB then pack rules; a deny blocks. On a prompt: pack text. ljos cards cards Read USER.md / MEMORY.md . Never writes. ljos policy -- ARGV policyd TCB then pack rules. A deny blocks. A check is the argv verdict. ljos consensus ID consensus crate DeGroot / ODE, then the tracker verb. MCP ljos-mcp execs ljos . Tool names match the verbs, including ljos_vote . Tool Arguments Does ljos_remember text Standing knowledge. Never extract-on-write. ljos_prefer text Standing preference. Never extract-on-write. ljos_search query Retrieve via PACKSET_URL . ljos_evidence accession deedar evidence. ljos_current accession deedar current tip. ljos_deed issue , optional add Cite an accession on a tracker node. ljos_recall issue Working set. ljos_claim node Claim a claimdag node. ljos_complete node Complete a claimdag node. docs.title: Sit and finish
docs.text: Skip to content Open a ticket. Print the island. An island is the cluster of linked claims this task activates. The ticket stays open until vissue closes it. Overview First write Sit Policy Harnesses Crates Alternatives Reference 1. Point at scratch stores A first sitting should not touch a live tracker. Make an empty tracker directory in a fresh scratch directory, export the roots, start the pack writer, and ask doctor. A tracker is a directory holding Software/ or a vissue.toml . mktemp -d gives a directory only you own; a fixed /tmp path can be another user's or left over from an earlier run, and git init then fails on its config lock. The tracker commits every change, so git needs an identity ( git config --global user.email ), or the commit is refused with Author identity unknown . $ seat=$(mktemp -d) && mkdir -p "$seat/tracker/Software" "$seat/deeds" $ git -C "$seat/tracker" init -q && cd "$seat" $ export VISSUE_ROOT="$seat/tracker" DEEDAR_URL="file://$seat/deeds" $ export CLAIMDAG_DIR="$seat/claims" PACKSET_URL=http://127.0.0.1:18761 $ packsetd --port 18761 --home "$seat/pack" & $ ljos doctor 2. Make a ticket and sit it sitting prints its sections in order and stops at the first store that does not answer: doctor, sync, cards, due, the island the title activates, open blockers, the playbook it binds, the panel when the issue is a decision, recall, timeline, then the claim. Sync pulls the tracker and takes the other machines' sealed memory logs before the island is walked. On a decision issue the panel section writes one brief per persona the title names; each brief starts a subagent that casts one ballot as that persona, and finish --close refuses a decision with fewer than two ballots. When the tracker is a git checkout, the claim is committed and pushed, so another host sees who holds the ticket. After the sitting, read each due row and run ljos graded ID (or --lapsed ). The clock does not move until you grade. --assignee is for a named worker. Left off, or given as a pronoun ( you , seat , agent ), the holder is this conversation's: the seat tagged with its process, the same in the runner's tools and its shells ( ljos seat prints it). Occupancy is holder:issue , so two conversations do not share one slot and a second sitting does not release the first. $ id=$(vissue create -p demo "Ship the fuse change?" -q) $ ljos sitting $id == doctor ... == timeline ... == claim gen=2 3. Cite what the work produced A deed is frozen bytes. The ticket cites the accession. Citing a deed names it; the bytes stay in deedar. $ echo 'fn main() {}' > patch.rs $ deedar create file --name "the fuse patch" --path patch.rs --agent you $ ljos deed $id --add deed-file-the-fuse-patch 4. Finish A lesson an agent writes is a proposal until it is accepted: finish prints its id, and ljos accept ID makes it live. The island fires when its seeds agree. The session node completes. An outcome, when named, rewrites trust. The ticket keeps its state until ljos finish $id --close or the tracker closes it. When the tracker is a git checkout, finish commits the ticket's file and pushes it, and the last line says which; this scratch tracker has no remote, so the push is refused and the commit stays local. A closure that stays in one working tree does not exist for any other host. $ ljos finish $id --lesson "The fuse patch shipped as one file. Nothing else moved." proposed 1735... as agent-derived; `ljos accept 1735...` writes it ... completed the session node for demo-... as done the ticket demo-... keeps its state; `ljos finish demo-... --close` or `vissue update demo-... -s DONE` closes it when the work is accepted tracker git: committed chore(issues): demo-... finished; push refused: fatal: No configured push destination. $ ljos accept 1735... Agreement is ljos consensus over ljos-consensus on crates.io. The seat crate walks the same loop: ljos getting started . Field note: completing is not closing .

docs.title: First write
docs.text: Skip to content Write one claim. Search it back. A reader who has never used the seat finishes this page with one lesson in the pack. Search returns the same text. A review clock is running on it. Overview First write Sit Policy Harnesses Crates Alternatives Reference 1. Install $ cargo binstall ljos packset Without cargo-binstall , cargo install ljos packset is the same. Other runners: Harnesses . Work starts as a ticket. vissue q -p PROJECT "TITLE" mints it in the tracker VISSUE_ROOT names, and ljos sitting claims it. That tracker is yours. A ticket filed on one machine is invisible to every other install until VISSUE_ROOT is a git checkout those machines share. The sit page uses a scratch tracker under /tmp so a first run does not touch a live one. 2. Write one claim, then retrieve it $ ljos remember "the default fuse is CombMNZ" 8e3e7827... lesson due 2026-10-10T21:56:09.549Z the default fuse is CombMNZ $ ljos search fuse Score is how the scorers ranked this query. ... 1.0000 3/3 lesson 8e3e7827... today the default fuse is CombMNZ ljos remember starts the writer when none is answering. PACKSET_URL=off is the one way to have no pack. A URL pointed somewhere else is not replaced. 3. The clock $ ljos due 0 due; 1 scheduled, next at ... Search shows kind lesson and the same sentence. A review is scheduled a day out. Tomorrow ljos due lists the claim. ljos graded ID (or --lapsed ) moves the clock. 4. Prefer is the same path $ ljos prefer "never extract on write" $ ljos search extract Score is how the scorers ranked this query. ... 2.0000 3/3 preference fe9d4d04... today never extract on write 1.0000 1/3 lesson 8e3e7827... today the default fuse is CombMNZ The fraction is how many of the scorers named the hit. Neither number says whether the claim is true. Next: sit and finish . The crate tutorial runs memory, agreement, and a handover: ljos getting started .

docs.title: The pin is an accession.
docs.text: Skip to content The pin is an accession. Back to the field DEEDAR_URL names the directory ( file:// plus a path). Unset, the command has nowhere to write. deedar create file needs --id , --path , and --agent . The pin is deed-… or sha256: . ljos evidence asks deedar for the bytes. ljos deed ID --add ACCESSION names the accession on a ticket. The product stays in deedar. The pack may name the same accession. Each habitat keeps the name. If the store is empty, that is an error. Frozen product / deedar

docs.title: The settle is the consensus.
docs.text: Skip to content The settle is the consensus. Back to the field ljos vote ID --for OPTION records a ballot. One ballot per identity; --as NAME casts as a persona. A recast replaces. A missing identity is no. ljos consensus ID is the seat verb: the model crate, then the tracker, both under the trust rows the pack holds that apply to the issue's topic and every persona's anchor. The model is DeGroot / Friedkin–Johnsen, or bounded confidence when the issue is tagged broad , or the Seldon ODE when --seldon and seldon are on PATH. Every outcome says how the group split, in polarization and disagreement; a count says only who won. On a hard question add a forecast beside the ballot, ljos predict ID --expect OPTION ; with two or more forecasts the settle also names the surprisingly popular answer, the option whose actual share most exceeds its forecast, and shows each voter's standing from the rows. The rows are memory. ljos learn ID --outcome OPTION weighs each voter by its record's accuracy, shrunk toward the panel's pooled accuracy, keeps the outcome, and loosens the anchors of refuted personas; ljos calibrate -p PROJECT writes rows from the project's history when nobody names an outcome; ljos trust FROM TO W --about DOMAIN sets one by hand, scoped. ljos consensus discounts the voters who err together once five issues have an outcome. Under equal rows a settle is a count. A panel is one subagent per persona, each started from ljos brief NAME ID , each casting one ballot as itself, then the settle. ljos persona NAME --anchor A --view TEXT --about DOMAIN writes the persona once; it stays in the pack. Where the machine turned Jev on, ljos panel ID --jev asks Jev for each persona's ballot first. Jev returns what the ballot always carried and a subagent had to guess: the chosen option's probability is the confidence, and its forecast of the panel is the prediction, so the settle and the surprisingly popular reading need nothing new. Personas answered by one model are one correlated voter, so the panel casts only when every seat is sure (confidence 0.8 or above) and all agree. Otherwise it casts nothing and writes the briefs, and the subagents take the contested question. learn scores a Jev ballot like any other. Four green ticks are a host rule for landing work. They are not the model. Do not report a count as if it were the crate. The explanation is where a settle's claim comes from: the closed form the iteration solves for, the round count guaranteed for an anchored settle, the SymPy check and the interval enclosure under Derivations, proofs and certificates, and when to use each model. consensus · ljos · seldon-code

docs.title: A check is the argv verdict.
docs.text: Skip to content A check is the argv verdict. Back to the field $ uvx ljos-policyd check -- uv run pytest allow $ ljos-policyd capnp -- true | wc -c 40 The typed verdict is Cap'n PolicyDecision (phronesis; Ali Akber Saifee / indynull, HaoZeke). A Janet pack can deny more after that verdict: (defn check [argv] (when (has-prefix? (get argv 0) "sudo") (deny "sudo"))) ljos-policyd check -- argv is the TCB when the binary is on PATH (or POLICYD_BIN ). It prints allow or deny . capnp writes the packed message. The harness hook and ljos policy call it. The Janet pack may only deny more. ljos policy -- argv prints the line, then the TCB verdict if the binary answered, then any pack rule that matches, then what the pack knows that bears on it. The binary prints a verdict. Pack rules stay in packset. A missing binary leaves the line open unless POLICYD_REQUIRED=1 . Doctor names the row. ljos hook on PreToolUse is the same gate. A deny is a blocked tool call: $ echo '{"hook_event_name":"PreToolUse","tool_input":{"command":"git push --force"}}' | ljos hook {"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"PreToolUse","permissionDecision":"deny","permissionDecisionReason":"git-force-push (seat rule `ljos-policyd`)"}} On a prompt it searches and holds pack text; PostToolUse emits it. Nothing to say on a prompt is no output. A TCB deny still blocks. ljos onboard installs it on a runner's tool-call and prompt events. When the session ends, the memories the hook injected during it fire together, so what served one sitting is wired for the next. Law can live in the pack: ljos rule 'PATTERN' --verdict deny|ask --why "..." writes a glob over the command line with a verdict, and the hook returns it as the runner's permission decision while ljos policy prints it beside the line. A rule is memory: dated, supersedable, exported in handovers. A pack rule is tried on the whole line and on each command the line runs. The line splits on && , || , ; , | and & outside quotes, and leading NAME=value assignments and sudo , env , time , nohup come off, so cd repo && git push meets git push* and a commit message that names a command does not. A pattern that says re: , or carries \b , \s , \d , \w or an alternation group, is a regular expression anchored at the command's start. Edit a pack rule only when argv law itself changes. Do not write comments, dates, ticket ids, or sitting notes into it. If the binary is down, leave the pack rules alone. Other projects may speak one habitat and ignore ljos . Habitats · Compare

docs.title: Overflow is an error.
docs.text: Skip to content Overflow is an error. Back to the field ljos cards prints USER.md and MEMORY.md from --dir (default . ). A missing file prints nothing. The command never creates those files and never writes them. Cards answer one question: what did the human freeze? Overflow is an error, not a prompt to dump more. A client scrapbook is not a card. Read the cards at the start of a sitting. If they are empty, leave them empty. Habitats

docs.text: Skip to content Citing a deed names it; the bytes stay in deedar. Open the note for the thing you are about to do. It names the verb, the contract, and the failure that looks like success. cards What the human froze. Read-only. packset Standing knowledge. Written only on Remember: / Prefer: . deedar Frozen product. Opened by accession. vissue The graph and the agreement. Docs: vissue.rgoswami.me . claimdag Work for this sitting. The ticket stays open until vissue closes it. policyd Argv law is the command-line verdict. ljos policy prints the line. ljos-policyd is the TCB when it is on PATH or POLICYD_BIN . A check is the argv verdict. ljos hook injects memory at the point of action. Docs: ljos-policyd . consensus DeGroot / Friedkin–Johnsen. The settle is the consensus. Notes Write – Remember is a speech act Cards – Overflow is an error Accession – The pin is an accession Session – The ticket stays open Agreement – The settle is the consensus Argv – A check is the argv verdict; memory at the point of action Compare – A memory engine is one habitat

docs.title: The ticket stays open.
docs.text: Skip to content The ticket stays open. Back to the field ljos sitting ISSUE [--assignee NAME] opens the sitting: doctor, cards, due, island, recall, timeline, claim, in that order, stopping at the first store that does not answer. The name defaults to this conversation's holder, the seat tagged with its process ( ljos seat prints it); a named worker passes its own. Occupancy is holder and issue: one live claim per holder per issue. A second claim is refused with the issue the name still holds and the two verbs that free it: ljos complete finishes it, ljos release hands it back unfinished. ljos finish ISSUE --lesson "..." [--outcome OPTION] closes the sitting: remember, fire the island, complete, learn. A later sitting on the same issue reopens its node and takes it; the ledger keeps the earlier completion. The ticket stays open until vissue closes it. The tracker is the graph. Create and claim tickets through vissue . Never hand-edit issues.org . Crate docs: vissue.rgoswami.me . File before you speak. An audit with no ids is unfinished work. A leftover that does not fit this sitting is a child ticket, then the original work continues. Session work / claimdag

docs.title: Remember is a speech act.
docs.text: Skip to content Remember is a speech act. Back to the field ljos remember POSTs one lesson to /v1/atoms . ljos prefer POSTs one preference. The writer is found on 127.0.0.1:8761 with nothing set; packset ensure starts one. A writer that is down is an error, never an empty pack. The seat's memory is one workspace, seat , from any directory. The pack's own command line keys a workspace to the git remote of the directory it stands in; the seat does not, because a seat is one memory across every repository it works in. PACKSET_WORKSPACE names another on purpose. Search is GET /v1/search on the seat's workspace. It does not open a deed. A transcript is not a source. If you did not say Remember: or Prefer: , the pack did not change. Every recalled memory carries its age ( [lesson, 3 weeks ago] ), and the hook's lessons run oldest to newest behind the preferences; read them as a timeline, a later one revises an earlier one. ljos timeline ISSUE is the tracker's logbook, the cited deeds and the activated memories as one dated list, oldest first, with the gap between lines. ljos search TOPIC --as-of TIME is the pack as it stood then. A lesson that rewrites an earlier one (same opening words, a new object) closes the earlier one's window on arrival, and remember says so. ljos consolidate runs the same rule over what is already held and reports the pairs; --apply closes them. Run it after ljos receive --import . ljos island CUE is what a task touches; ljos hubs is what the pack turns on by its own links, a weighted PageRank over them: the natural list to pin, to review first, or to carry when the whole pack is too much. Every claim enters the review clock on write. ljos due lists what is due and ends with one line on the clock; ljos graded ID moves it. A claim never graded sinks in search as its retrievability falls. If packset status says up and remember hangs or returns 400, the writer is wedged. packset stop , then packset ensure . Do not dump the sitting into a card. Privacy-of-write

docs.title: Write one claim. Search it back.
docs.text: Skip to content Write one claim. Search it back. ljos gives coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor a memory, a work tracker, and a check on every shell command. It writes one claim when you say Remember: or Prefer:, then searches that claim back. Nothing is mined from chat, and memory stays on your machine unless you turn on a remote judge. Write one claim How sitting works Source Fig. 1 A sitting, in the order ljos prints it. The ticket stays open until vissue closes it. specimen sitting remember policy $ ljos sitting demo-k29f == doctor == sync == cards == due == island == blockers == playbook == recall == timeline == claim gen=2 install Copy cargo binstall ljos packset ljos remember "the default fuse is CombMNZ" ljos search fuse ljos remember starts the writer when none is answering. The walk: First write . The name: leiðarljós . Why this exists Agents forget, remember the wrong things, and run any command. They forget Each session starts cold. The fix you agreed on yesterday, the rule about force pushes, the reason a test is skipped: gone unless someone pastes it back in. Auto-memory fills with things nobody said Tools that mine the transcript keep whatever a model guessed was worth keeping, including text that came from a web page or a tool result. That is how memory gets poisoned. Shell commands run unchecked A coding agent with a shell can push, delete, or pipe a download into sh on its own judgement. ljos writes a memory only when you say Remember: or Prefer: , keeps it in plain local files you can read, and checks each shell command against fixed rules before it runs. No model sits in the write path or the check, and it all runs on a CPU. The loop Sit, work, finish. Fig. 2 The sitting loop and the five stores it reads and writes. Every store is a local file or a loopback service. 01 Sit ljos sitting ID opens the ticket: doctor, sync, cards, due, island, blockers, playbook, recall, timeline, then the claim. It refuses a ticket with open blockers. 02 Work ljos note logs progress on the ticket. deedar create records what the work produced, and ljos deed cites it. ljos remember and ljos prefer are the only memory writes. 03 Finish ljos finish ID remembers the lesson, fires the island, completes the session node, and learns from an outcome when one is named. The ticket stays open until vissue closes it. cards USER.md , MEMORY.md What the human froze. ljos prints these two files and never writes them. sit reads pack packset Lessons and preferences, one claim each, searched back per prompt. sit reads · work and finish write tracker vissue Tickets as plain Org files in a git repository. sit reads · work notes · finish completes deeds deedar A hashed record of each artefact the work produced. work writes · the ticket cites claims claimdag One live claim per holder per ticket. A second claim on a held ticket is refused. sit claims · finish completes ljos words: a seat is one agent runner on one machine, with its memory and claims. A sitting is one piece of work on one ticket. A deed is a hashed record of what that work produced. packset is the memory store that search reads, and vissue is the tracker, plain Org files in git. leiðarljós is Icelandic for a guiding light. Fig. 3 One sitting on a fresh seat, about a minute long. A script types the commands; every line of output is real. The script is demo.sh . The recording needs JavaScript. The raw cast is ljos-demo.cast , playable with asciinema play . Fig. 4 LongMemEval_S, n = 470 answerable questions, session retrieval. CombMNZ fuses BM25+ with multilingual-e5-large; the default install encodes with bge-small-en-v1.5, and without the encoder search stays lexical. Writes only on Remember: and Prefer:. arm recall@5 QA / ceiling BM25+ lexical 0.914 — CombMNZ fused 0.949 0.549 / 0.634 QA for CombMNZ fused uses a local 7 B reader and judge, top five sessions, against the labelled-session ceiling. Compare · packset explanation . Fig. 5 Install cost of the same local stack, packset and ljos, built with cargo install from crates.io on one 8-thread Xeon with two build jobs. Lexical search, no encoder. build, both crates 4 min 20 s binaries on disk 45 MB packsetd resident 15 MB search p50 / p95 3.3 / 4.1 ms 281 claims in the pack, one process per query. Method, script and raw logs . Contents Each store has its own site. This page teaches sitting. Those pages teach the crate. Org plus Sphinx, the same shape as vissue . ljos What does this seat do next? I packset What does this seat know, standing? II deedar What did this unit of work produce?
